title: Changing Values (var)
story: You're playing a video game and your score keeps going up as you collect coins. You can't use `let` for that — `let` locks the value forever! You need a special kind of variable that CAN change. That's `var`.
why: Mutable variables let programs track changing state like scores, health bars, counts, and positions — the heart of every game and app.
analogy: `let` is a tattoo — permanent and unchanging. `var` is a whiteboard — you can erase and rewrite whenever you want.
try_it: Start with 100 points, subtract 15 (you lost a life), then add 30 (you found a treasure). Print the score after each change so you can watch it go up and down!
tips: Default to `let` — only use `var` when you know the value needs to change later
You can change a `var` as many times as you want — there's no limit!
When reassigning, DON'T write the type again: just `points = 85;`, not `var points: Int = 85;`
common_mistakes: Trying to reassign a `let` variable — the compiler won't allow it. Switch to `var` instead!
Writing the full declaration when reassigning: `var score: Int = 50;` creates a NEW variable. Just write `score = 50;`
